newsitem.title: USA: Health proposals key to U.S. tobacco settlement.
newsitem.headline: Health proposals key to U.S. tobacco settlement.

text.p: A key congressional foe of smoking said Friday that recommendations from health groups for a tobacco settlement are probably more significant than those from top state legal officers.

"I'm most interested in recommendations from the public health community," Representative Henry Waxman of California said in an interview. "I think what Doctors (C. Everett) Koop and (David) Kessler may be recommending is more significant than what the attorneys general and the tobacco industry may recommend."
Waxman, an influential Democrat, was in New York to speak at a conference for portfolio managers.

His comments followed Thursday's meeting of a group of anti-smoking advocates who are trying ensure that public health, not money and liability, form the heart of any negotiated settlement between states and the tobacco industry.
The group, the Advisory Committee on Tobacco Policy and Public Health, was formed at the request of some congressional critics of the tobacco industry.
It is headed by Koop, the former U.S. Surgeon General, and Kessler, the former Commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration.

Health groups and some members of Congress are concerned that state attorneys general are moving too quickly towards a settlement that would give cigarette makers too much immunity from lawsuits and would provide inadequate funds to pay for damages, smoking-cessation and education programmes.
The attorneys general are planning to gather on Tuesday in Dallas to discuss developments in the talks and negotiations with the industry are expected to resume afterwards.
Waxman said that, even if the attorneys general and the industry reached an agreement shortly, any pact would still have to be approved by Congress.
Both House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott expressed doubts this week about whether it would be possible to get a bill through Congress this year.
Waxman said he was very pleased that Koop and Kessler were willing to take on the task of producing proposals from the health community.
The panel agreed to work swiftly and will convene again in two weeks with proposals regarding education, health, research, taxation and regulation.
Waxman said there was no reason to rush to a settlement simply because the first of the state trials aiming to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers is scheduled to begin next month.
"That doesn't make sense to me," he said.

A group of attorneys general, plaintiffs lawyers and members of the health care industry began negotiating with tobacco officials in early April in an effort to resolve litigation against cigarette makers in exchange for major health and monetary concessions.

Mississippi's case is scheduled to be the first to go to trial, on July 7, and the state's attorney general, Mike Moore, a key negotiator, hoped to know by next week whether a deal could be reached or if he should get ready for trial.
A total of 33 states have sued cigarette makers in a bid to recoup health care costs of smokers, with New Hampshire filing its suit on Wednesday.
Eleven states have joined the battle since settlement talks began and it is expected that Oregon and California will also sue the industry.
